children: A Department of Defense memo is reportedly curbing casual contact between U.S. and Canadian uniformed personnel, Sen.
Mike Rounds
(R-S.D.) said on Saturday.

At the Halifax International Security Forum in Nova Scotia, Rounds said the guidance was drafted months ago and only signed more recently, and he said it doesn’t touch operational frameworks such as NORAD, NATO or the Five Eyes, according to a report by The Hill.
Rounds described it as a clampdown on informal interactions between American and Canadian officers.
Canada’s Trade Talks: A Tipping Point?
The timing lands as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney argues

params.linkText: Canada could turn to Chinese automakers

children: if trade talks with President Donald Trump break down, a reminder that political friction can spill into areas that depend on day-to-day trust.

Carney pushed back on the idea that Canada’s outreach to China was a negotiating ploy, saying, “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.” He also said the Canadian market had become less integrated with the U.S. because of American trade actions. Ottawa continues to prioritize Washington but is exploring alternatives in Europe, China and Japan if negotiations fail.

Rounds said Canadian counterparts told the U.S. delegation they are working to lift defense spending, and he suggested the memo read like an attempt to apply pressure on that front. He also said Canadians told lawmakers the directive sounded consistent with what they had already been doing over roughly the past year and a half.
The economic backdrop Carney described has real exposure for automakers with plants spread across Canada, the U.S. and Mexico, including
Ford Motor Co.
General Motors Co.
and
Stellantis NV
. Canada has also threatened legal action after Stellantis shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Ontario to Illinois, underscoring how quickly disputes can escalate.
How US Policies Are Reshaping Defense Ties

Rounds said he doubted the memo was meant to be public and characterized it as a restatement of existing practice based on conversations with Canadians, according to the report. He said the delegation’s aim is to make sure similar directives aren’t needed going forward by rebuilding a stronger cooperative tone.
Democratic Sens.
Kirsten Gillibrand
Chris Coons
Tim Kaine
and
Andy Kim
joined Rounds at the forum and also addressed reporters Saturday. Kaine, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, criticized the memo’s approach, calling the tone bad and unnecessary.

Kaine said the policy traces back months and was essentially formalizing something that had already been in place, and he predicted the next Congress would shift the tenor of the relationship. Coons said he took comfort that the memo doesn’t disrupt operations, but he warned against widening the gap between two close partners while adversaries cooperate more closely.
Implications Of Strained U.S.-Canada Relations

Coons said the United States should do nothing to further aggravate the distance and division between the two countries, while pointing to closer cooperation among Iran, North Korea, China and Russia.

Carney has also pointed to ongoing talks with Trump and senior U.S. officials, saying Saturday that discussions had moved forward even though disagreements remained. Trump, in a Fox News interview on November 3, said, “We’re going to make a deal with Canada very soon."

Canada’s trade posture has already included tariff changes with China under a January agreement that reduced duties on a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles from 100% to 6.1% with an initial cap of 49,000 imports a year, while China eased tariffs on Canadian agricultural goods.
Ontario Premier
Doug Ford
has criticized Chinese EV inflows, warning they could put auto jobs and U.S. market access at risk amid wider manufacturing disputes.
